problems.source_says: The anchoring score is computed on each story. In the AI arms the story was written while GPT-4 ideas were available, and the form itself codes ai_available_when_produced 'yes' and construct 'other'. Codebook section 1 then gives with_ai: 'An outcome produced with AI available is across_people when its construct is diversity and with_ai otherwise.' The codebook has no 'none' code. The form-spec allows 'none' for outcomes that answer none of the three questions, and its example is AI output compared with human output. This score is not that case: it is computed on stories that people wrote, and the paper uses it to explain why AI-arm stories are more alike. If the screeners judge that it answers none of the questions, form-spec rule 7 does not call for listing it, and the result belongs in notes. Fix: recode to with_ai, or drop the outcome and keep the result in notes.
problems.quote: To understand why generative AI-inspired stories look more similar to each other, it is instructive to take a closer look at the relationship between generative AI ideas and the stories produced.
problems.locator: p. 4, Results, 'Similarity of stories', last paragraph of the right column (continues on p. 5, left column); codebook section 1; form-spec field note on 'question' and rule 7

problems.form_value: Not coded as outcomes. S1-O1 measure_detail: 'Component items plotted in Fig. 2A without printed numbers.' Notes: the components 'appear only in Fig. 2A and are folded into the index outcomes.'
problems.source_says: Fig. 2A plots its own estimate and interval for each component (novel, original, rare; appropriate, feasible, publishable) in each AI arm. Each is an evaluator rating of a story written with AI available, so each bears on with_ai. Form-spec rule 7 folds only robustness variants into one outcome, and these are separate rated items. Without S1-O10 (coded none) and S1-O11 (not scored on output), the paper has 15 outcomes that are scored on the output and bear on a question (2 indices, 6 components, 6 exploratory items, 1 similarity), so all fit under the 15-outcome cap. The components carry information that the index rows do not: in the one-idea arm the intervals for 'Original' and 'Appropriate' cross zero and the one for 'Feasible' reaches zero, while both index intervals exclude zero. This is minor: the preregistered indices stay the primary records, and the components have no printed numbers (figure_only).
problems.quote: Compares novelty and usefulness indices (with constituent components of each index below) of participants in the Human-only condition (dashed vertical line) to participants who had access to one generative AI idea
problems.locator: p. 3, Fig. 2A and its caption (one-idea rows read at 12x zoom); p. 8, 'Outcome variables', 'Creativity'; form-spec rule 7

confirmed: S1-O1, S1-O2, and S1-O4 to S1-O9 are ratings of each story by a separate sample of 600 Prolific evaluators, who were not told the conditions. They are scored on the output and are not self-reports (p. 2, left column, paragraph beginning 'In the second phase'; p. 2, Fig. 1 caption).

S1-O3 and S1-O10 are computed measures: cosine similarity of OpenAI embeddings, times 100. The paper does not name the embedding model (p. 4, 'Similarity of stories', first paragraph; p. 8, 'Similarity scores').

S1-O11 is the writers' rating of their own story. The form correctly codes it scored_on_output false and measure self_report, and its two 'no statistically significant differences' sentences match the text (p. 3, left column, third paragraph, table S5; p. 3, end of 'Exploratory analyses', table S7; p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', fourth paragraph).

AI ideas were available while each story was written in both AI arms: a three-sentence GPT-4 idea on request, visible to the writer, with no copy and paste. Every outcome is scored on that one story, so ai_available_when_produced 'yes' and timing 'immediate' hold for all 11 outcomes. No outcome is produced after AI is removed, so no after_ai record is missing (p. 2, left column, paragraph beginning 'In our Human-only baseline condition'; p. 7, 'Writer study and experimental conditions', third paragraph).

Question codes follow the codebook rule for every outcome except S1-O10: with_ai for S1-O1, S1-O2, S1-O4 to S1-O9, and S1-O11 (AI available, construct other than diversity), and across_people for S1-O3 (AI available, diversity) (codebook section 1).

S1-O3 compares each story with the average embedding of all other stories in the same condition. Each writer wrote one story, so the measure compares different people's outputs. The construct is diversity, not flexibility (p. 8, 'Similarity scores', last sentence; p. 8, 'Statistical analysis': 'each writer produces one story').

S1-O3's direction 'treatment_lower' reverses the similarity sign into diversity terms, and the record says so, as codebook section 7 requires. The paper reports both AI arms as more similar (p. 4, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph).

Construct codes for the exploratory items follow the codebook term lists: well written as usefulness ('quality'), surprising twist as novelty ('surprise'), and enjoyable, boring, funny, and changed expectations as other. The paper keeps all six outside its novelty index (novel, original, rare) and its usefulness index (appropriate, feasible, publishable). Its Jauss motivation for 'changed expectations' makes novelty a defensible alternative, and the form records this (p. 8, 'Outcome variables', 'Creativity'; p. 3, 'Exploratory analyses', first paragraph).

Units are the paper's own. Evaluator outcomes are regressed per evaluation with SEs clustered by evaluator (unit rating; 3519 evaluations of 293 stories by 600 evaluators). Writer-study outcomes are regressed per story with robust SEs (unit output; 293 stories). The main text prints these totals, not a per-regression N (p. 8, 'Statistical analysis'; p. 8, paragraph beginning 'There were a total of 3519 evaluations').

Measure codes hold. The evaluators are 'regular' Prolific readers, 'not selected on the basis of prior experience in the publishing industry' (human_raters). The two similarity outcomes are embedding_similarity (p. 7, 'Evaluator study', first paragraph; p. 8, 'Similarity scores').

The index numbers match the PDF exactly: novelty 5.4% (b = 0.207, P = 0.021) and 8.1% (b = 0.311, P < 0.001); usefulness 3.7% (b = 0.185, P = 0.039), 9.0% (b = 0.453, P < 0.001), and five versus one 5.1% (P = 0.0012, one-idea mean 5.21) (p. 2, foot of right column, continuing on p. 3, left column, first and second paragraphs).

The exploratory numbers match the PDF exactly: enjoyable b = 0.216 (P = 0.028) and 0.375 (P < 0.001); twist 0.384 and 0.468 (both P < 0.001); well written 0.372 (P < 0.001); expectations 0.251 (P = 0.005); boring -0.200 (P = 0.049); funny -0.106 (P = 0.115) (p. 3, 'Exploratory analyses: Emotional characteristics', second paragraph).

The similarity numbers match the PDF exactly: similarity to other stories b = 0.871 (P < 0.001) and b = 0.718 (P = 0.003), an 8.10-point Human-only range, and 10.7 and 8.9 percent of it; similarity to the AI idea 5.2% (b = 4.29, P < 0.001, Human-only mean 82.85) and 5.0% (b = 4.11, P < 0.001) (p. 4, 'Similarity of stories', second paragraph; p. 5, left column, first paragraph).

Fig. 2B, read at 12x zoom: the one-idea intervals for well written (point about 0.12) and changed expectations (about 0.14) are positive and cross zero. The one-idea intervals for boring and funny (about -0.06 each) are negative and cross zero. These match the four figure-only rows coded no_clear_difference (p. 3, Fig. 2B).

Fig. 2A and Fig. 4B plot the printed b values (novelty 0.207 and 0.311, usefulness 0.185 and 0.453, similarity 0.871 and 0.718, AI-idea similarity 4.29 and 4.11), so 'figure_only' refers to the plotted intervals (p. 3, Fig. 2A; p. 5, Fig. 4B).

The one-idea novelty and usefulness contrasts are coded treatment_higher. The printed P values (0.021 and 0.039) and the Fig. 2A index intervals, which both exclude zero, support this. One caveat the form does not record: p. 2 says the 'statistically significant differences in our preregistered indices' come from the five-ideas arm (p. 2, right column, last paragraph; p. 3, left column).

The preregistered test of Human-only against the combined AI arms is reported only by direction, with numbers in section S4, so statistics_available 'none' is right for both combined contrasts (p. 2, Results, 'Baseline versus generative AI conditions', first paragraph).
The five-versus-one usefulness contrast is ai_design, because codebook section 5 lists 'one idea versus five' (p. 3, left column, second paragraph).

No other main-text outcome bears on the three questions. The DAT heterogeneity (Fig. 3) re-estimates the same outcomes in subgroups. The AI-authorship guesses, ownership, profit-split, and ethics items are perceptions, and their results sit in section S5 (p. 2, Fig. 1 caption and right column; pp. 3-4; p. 6, left column).
summary: The form codes c006's outcomes correctly in substance: the evaluator ratings and embedding similarities are scored on the stories, AI ideas were available while writing, the units match the paper's analysis, S1-O3 compares different writers' stories, and every printed number matches pp. 3 to 5. The conclusion is still refuted, because S1-O10 (similarity to a GPT-4 idea) is coded question 'none' where the codebook rule gives with_ai, and because the six Fig. 2A index components are folded into the indices although form-spec rule 7 folds only robustness variants.
